Volume 11 · Chapter 05

Liquidity, funding and asset-liability management

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c04

By the endAnalyze funding gaps and contingent cash needs across scenarios.

A payment needs usable money before its deadline

Capability. Build and reconcile a dated funding plan; stress its collateral, rollover and margin assumptions; prove the cash reserve needed by a fixed policy; and distinguish economic-value interest-rate risk from next-period income and payment liquidity. The prerequisite is market risk measurement. We also use the bank ledger in Chapter 2, dated bond values from Volume 10, Chapter 1, and the distinction between derivative settlements and margin funding from Volume 10, Chapter 5.

Bracken Bank expects to finish a short stress window with positive cash. Its securities have positive market value and its borrowers continue paying. Yet the proposed funding plan cannot meet an earlier deadline. The problem is neither solved by its final cash total nor diagnosed by a loss percentile alone. We need to know which money arrives, which obligations remain due, and which collateral can actually support a loan at each cutoff.

All numbers below are original synthetic teaching inputs. CU means domestic currency units; FU is a different currency used only in the fourth worked case. The main case is one legal entity, one settlement currency and four ordered cutoffs. A separate annual ALM book illustrates a different question. Neither book represents an observed institution, a regulatory liquidity ratio, a current accounting standard or a calibrated probability of distress.

1. Turn an inventory into a dated plan

Funding liquidity concerns meeting cash obligations when due. Market liquidity concerns executing asset trades at specified prices and sizes. A security can be valuable but inaccessible to today's settlement account; selling it and borrowing against it are different transactions. An expected future inflow is not a receipt at an earlier cutoff. The useful unit of analysis is therefore a legal entity, currency, account and time, with the rights to transfer between them stated explicitly.

What belongs in a liquidity ladder?
ItemTreatmentEvidence or assumption needed
Contractual loan principalCash inflow and reduction of loans when receivedPayment date, collection performance and settlement availability
Demand depositsScenario withdrawals reduce cash and deposit liabilitiesBehavioral runoff assumption; a contractual right to withdraw is not a forecast
Maturing wholesale borrowingOld principal remains due; any new loan is a separate inflowConfirmed amount, conditions and time of new financing
Undrawn customer commitmentA permitted draw can become cash outflow and a new loan assetExercise rights, capacity and timing; no automatic loss of the amount advanced
Pledged or restricted assetsContinue to exist on the balance sheet, but cannot be freely reusedEncumbrance, eligibility, custodian, location, release conditions and lead time
Derivative margin and settlementFollow the stipulated contract's cash transfersSegregation, netting rights, eligible collateral, interest and return dates

The BCBS's September 2008 international liquidity principles provide historical method context for projected cash flows, contingent demands, transfer constraints, collateral location and execution time. They do not establish that a particular facility will lend to Bracken. The April 2013 credit-line manuscript by Acharya and coauthors, already studied in Volume 8, gives a reason to investigate monitoring and conditions on access. Our numerical facility rules are stipulated contracts, not estimates from that paper.

A ladder has two distinct layers: cash assumptions and management actions. Deposit runoff and customer draws can vary by scenario. A policy specifies how much new funding to request, which collateral to pledge, when to repay and whether to sell. Do not silently substitute a different policy when a scenario becomes uncomfortable. Record both the original result and the altered plan.

2. A precise fixed-policy cash minimum

Let s index finitely many scenarios and j=1,…,m index all relevant payment cutoffs. Let C be initial unrestricted cash, Isj the usable receipts and Osj the payments at cutoff j. Include loan proceeds, principal repayments, interest, margin and asset purchases in the correct I or O. Under a stipulated policy, define the cumulative cash headroom with no new reserve:

Hsj(0)=C+Σk=1j(Isk−Osk).
b* = max{0, maxs,j[−Hsj(0)]}.

Proposition. Suppose (i) all listed receipts are legally and operationally available before the payments in their bucket; (ii) there is no other intermediate deadline; (iii) collateral, funding and counterparties deliver the specified receipts without first requiring an unmodeled payment; (iv) an extra b≥0 arrives as unrestricted cash before cutoff 1, remains available without interest or issuance cost, and carries no repayment during the horizon; and (v) adding b changes none of the other cash flows, rights or policy choices. Then all payments in all stated scenarios can be met if and only if b≥b*. Here b is an amount of cash; in the lab it is financed by an equal cash-equity contribution.

Proof. Induction on j gives Hsj(b)=Hsj(0)+b: the initial balance increases by b and every subsequent net flow is unchanged. If b<b*, some prefix has negative headroom, so its cumulative payments exceed its available resources; the plan fails. If b≥b*, every cutoff closes at a nonnegative balance. At a cutoff, all its receipts arrive before its payments; starting from the preceding nonnegative balance, sequential payment cannot cross below the closing balance because each payment reduces cash. Thus every intermediate payment in that bucket also succeeds. This proves sufficiency and necessity, including equality at zero headroom. For a finite nonempty scenario set the maximum is attained; if all original prefixes are nonnegative, b*=0.

This is a worst-case certificate for the specified finite set, not a probability forecast or an optimal funding policy. Split a day into more cutoffs if payment order matters. Maintain separate ladders where currency or entity transfers are restricted. If a facility's draw changes with b, or b itself has a repayment date, the additive identity must be rederived. For example, if b is instead borrowed initially and repaid as (1+g)b at the final cutoff, the earlier headrooms increase by b, but the last becomes Hsm(0)−gb. An initially helpful bridge can create its own maturity problem. A single end-of-period total does not settle feasibility.

3. Worked case 1: refinancing is a new loan

Bracken's opening ledger is below. Security amounts equal units because the stipulated book amount is 1 CU per unit. Of 80 units, 20 already secure obligations that remain encumbered throughout this window; 10 are in inaccessible custody throughout the window; only 50 may support the new secured facility. The 4 CU restricted cash remains unavailable. Initial margin of 5 was posted before the opening balance sheet and is a separate asset. There is no allowance or new loan impairment in this short case; all stated loan repayments are received.

Opening book balance, before an optional cash-equity contribution
AssetsCULiabilities and equityCU
Cash, including restricted 420Deposits160
Loans150Maturing wholesale principal40
Securities80Previously accrued wholesale interest payable0.4
Segregated initial margin5Other liabilities30
Total assets255Book equity24.6
Total liabilities and equity255

The chosen funding policy requests a secured loan of 30 at cutoff 1. The initial price is 1 and haircut 20%, so one eligible unit supports 0.8 CU principal. Capacity is 50(0.8)=40 and the draw pledges 30/0.8=37.5 units, leaving 12.5 eligible units free. The lender covers principal only in its collateral test; interest is separately payable. This is an explicit teaching contract, not a claim about every repo or secured lending agreement.

The old wholesale loan pays 40 principal and 0.4 already-accrued interest at cutoff 1 regardless of refinancing. If lenders offer a fraction ρ of its old principal as a new term loan, the policy accepts R=40ρ at cutoff 1 and repays R at cutoff 4. The new loan charges 0.5% per each of the three stated intervals; the secured loan charges 1% per interval on its opening principal. These are stipulated interval rates, not annualized market observations. New interest accrues at cutoffs 2, 3 and 4 and is paid at cutoff 4. The initial 0.4 payment is not a second expense.

All receipts shown for a cutoff arrive before its payments. Loan principal receipts are 0, 12, 18 and 40. The customer line, if drawn, pays principal back after this window. Six of the other liabilities mature at cutoff 3; the remaining 24 stay outstanding. No other funding, asset sales, taxes or income is assumed. The derivative settles variation gains or losses in cash at every cutoff and resets its remaining value to zero. Segregated initial margin earns no interest, cannot pay other obligations, and returns before cutoff-4 debt repayments when the derivative closes.

The secured interest is 3(0.01)(30)=0.9 and term interest is 3(0.005)(40)=0.6. All four prefixes are nonnegative; the fixed-policy extra cash minimum is zero. Ending total cash is 27.1+4=31.1; loans are 150−70=80; securities remain 80 and margin is zero. Thus assets are 191.1, liabilities are 142 deposits plus 24 other liabilities, and equity is 25.1. Now change only ρ from 1 to 0. The new 40 is missing at cutoff 1, but so are its final 40 repayment and 0.6 interest expense. The headrooms become −6.4, −1.4, 8.6, 27.7. Finishing with 27.7 does not rescue cutoff 1. A timely independent cash reserve of 6.4 makes the plan feasible under the fixed rules. Rows after a negative prefix are full-payment diagnostics: they show the algebra of the proposed plan, not an assertion that a bank may keep paying with negative usable cash. The model does not invent an overdraft, default waterfall or lender of last resort.

4. Worked case 2: collateral capacity and customer calls interact

At cutoff 2 the new secured facility rechecks collateral. Write Q for eligible units, p for the new price, h for the new haircut and D for principal before maintenance. Each unit supports a=(1−h)p CU. The policy pledges more of the eligible pool if needed; if the entire pool is insufficient, it pays down principal. Consequently:

Dafter=min{D,aQ};   principal paydown=max{0,D−aQ};
new pledged units=Dafter/a;   free eligible units=Q−Dafter/a.

We assume p>0 and h<1. This makes the unit requirement well defined. More eligible collateral or a smaller haircut weakly reduces the paydown, holding other terms fixed. The already-pledged 20 and inaccessible 10 do not enter Q. Falling market value and rising haircuts can act together: the haircut changes funding capacity and does not by itself establish a book loss. If transfer of the extra units is too late, use the smaller deliverable Q at the actual maintenance cutoff.

The joint stress has no wholesale refinancing. Deposit withdrawals are 16, 8, 7, 0; variation settlements are −3, −9, +5, +10. At cutoff 2 a customer exercises 12 of its 15 CU commitment, and required segregated initial margin rises from 5 to 9. Collateral price falls to 0.7 and the haircut rises to 30%. All 50 eligible units support only 24.5, so the 30 CU secured loan requires 5.5 principal paydown. All 50 units are then pledged. The remaining secured principal is unchanged until its cutoff-4 maturity.

Joint-stress cumulative cash, without an added reserve
CutoffNet-flow calculationClosing available CU
116 opening +30 secured −40.4 old debt −16 deposits −3 variation−13.4
2Previous +12 loans −8 deposits −12 customer draw −9 variation −4 extra initial margin −5.5 paydown−39.9
3Previous +18 loans −7 deposits −6 other liabilities +5 variation−29.9
4Previous +40 loans +10 variation +9 initial margin return −24.5 secured principal −0.79 interest3.81

The 0.79 interest is 0.01(30)+0.01(24.5)+0.01(24.5). At cutoff 2, interest for the completed interval is based on 30 before the paydown. Posting the extra 4 initial margin moves cash to a segregated asset; advancing 12 moves cash to loans; paying down 5.5 reduces cash and secured debt. None is an expense. Variation −9 is the stipulated derivative loss and cash payment; accrual of 0.3 interest reduces equity and creates a payable before its later cash payment. These different journal entries cannot be inferred from the identical sign of their cash effects.

The largest deficit is 39.9 at cutoff 2. Across the base, rollover-only and joint scenarios, b*=39.9. With that cash-equity contribution the joint headrooms become 26.5, 0, 10, 43.71; all three scenarios are feasible. Exactly zero at the binding cutoff is mathematically sufficient under the stated timing, but gives no slack for an omitted payment or execution delay.

Without the reserve, the full-payment closing diagnostic has cash 7.81 including restricted 4, loans 92, securities book value 80, deposits 129 and other liabilities 24. Its residual book equity is 26.81=24.6+3−0.79. If all securities are marked at 0.7 and every other account is explicitly valued at its book amount, the corresponding marked equity is 26.81−24=2.81. That is a conditional valuation, not freely spendable 2.81 CU, and it describes an infeasible proposed path unless the funding gap is repaired. With the feasible 39.9 cash-equity contribution, ending book equity is 66.71 and marked equity is 42.71. These calculations do not assume that the credit risk or economic discounting of the unchanged loan book has independently been estimated.

5. Worked case 3: value and next-year income move in opposite directions

Asset-liability management (ALM) coordinates asset and funding risks across dates. Economic value of equity (EVE) compares present values of assets and liabilities under a common valuation basis. Net interest income (NII) measures interest income less interest expense over a stated interval. Payment liquidity additionally asks whether actual cash reaches the correct account before each deadline. A rate reset changes the coupon schedule; it need not be the date when principal matures.

Consider a separate annual book with 10 unremunerated cash, an asset paying 5 in year 1 and 105 in year 2, a five-year fixed liability with face 80 and annual coupon 4, and a five-year floating liability with face 20. It has no credit spread, default, optionality, floor, taxes or transaction costs. At date 0 the floating coupon resets to 20y; under the flat-curve scenario all later annual coupons reset to that same amount. Principal 20 matures in year 5, not at the first coupon reset. The flat annual discount yield is y>−1.

PA(y)=5/(1+y)+105/(1+y)2;
PF(y)=Σt=154/(1+y)t+80/(1+y)5;
Pfloat(y)=Σt=1520y/(1+y)t+20/(1+y)5=20;
EVE(y)=10+PA(y)−PF(y)−20;
NIIyear 1(y)=5−4−20y=1−20y.

To verify the floating value, write y/(1+y)t=(1+y)−(t−1)−(1+y)−t. Summing telescopes to 1−(1+y)−5; adding discounted principal gives 1 times face 20. This proof includes y=0 without division by y. It relies on coupon resetting to the valuation rate with no credit spread; arbitrary floating liabilities need not remain at par.

Exact formulas evaluated at two flat annual yields; CU values rounded here
YieldAsset PVFixed liability PVFloating liability PVEVENext-year NII
5%1008020100
7%96.38396473.4396842012.944280−0.4

The same upward rate change raises EVE and lowers next-year NII. The longer fixed liability loses more value than the short asset, benefiting the residual claim, while the floating liability's next coupon becomes more expensive. These are different horizons and cash-flow sensitivities, not inconsistent accounts.

For fixed payments ct, termwise differentiation of a finite sum gives P′(y)=−Σ t ct/(1+y)t+1. At 5%, P′A≈−185.941043 and P′F≈−346.358134 CU per unit of yield, so EVE′≈160.417091, whereas NII′=−20. A one-percentage-point local change is 0.01 times a derivative; a basis point is 0.0001. The derivative is a local approximation. The exact two-percentage-point EVE gain is 2.944280, rather than 0.02(160.417091)=3.208342. Nonparallel curves, different reset bases, deposit behavior and option exercise require separate cash-flow assumptions; one duration or repricing gap does not resolve them.

Even an accurate annual NII calculation does not certify timely payments. If only 0.2 of the 10 cash is usable before the year-1 morning deadline, the 7% funding coupons of 4+1.4=5.4 require another 5.2 before that time. The asset's 5 coupon arriving that afternoon cannot meet the morning deadline. The remaining 9.8 is stipulated inaccessible until afterward; it still contributes to the stated value calculation. If all 10 were available in the morning, there would be no such funding gap. The restriction and timing, rather than the sign of EVE or NII, decide that question.

6. Worked case 4: group money and the settlement account

A domestic entity has 4 CU and owes 12 CU at 11:00. An affiliate owns 8 FU. At a stated conversion rate of 1.25 CU per FU, the potential conversion is 8 FU×1.25 CU/FU=10 CU. The multiplication converts units; it does not establish an executable transfer.

Three explicitly different transfer rights
PlanHeadroom at 11:00Conclusion
No authorized affiliate transfer4−12=−8 CUNeeds 8 timely CU; affiliate ownership does not create local cash
Authorized, operationally confirmed conversion settles at 10:004+10−12=2 CUPayment feasible under these rights
Same authorized proceeds settle at 12:004−12=−8 CULater diagnostic balance 2 does not repair the 11:00 failure

The timely case assumes the foreign cash is available to settle the conversion, all permissions are satisfied and no unlisted fee, collateral or preceding cash payment is required. Real currency conversion and intercompany transfers require their own terms. The lesson is to identify missing rights and dates, not to infer a particular jurisdiction's transfer rule. The same logic explains why the 10 inaccessible security units in Bracken's main case cannot fill a collateral call just because an asset register lists them.

7. What a credible funding decision adds

A liquidity ladder is a conditional decision tool. Write down the owner of each action, its amount and currency, the approval and settlement deadline, the asset it consumes, and its repayment or reversal. A sale has proceeds and removes an asset; a secured draw consumes collateral capacity and creates principal plus interest; a customer-line cancellation needs an actual right and may change customer behavior. An emergency facility requires eligible collateral, operational access and a willing or authorized provider. Merely naming an action supplies none of these.

Bracken's fixed policy deliberately still draws 30 secured even after a large cash-equity contribution. That makes the reserve proof transparent. It does not minimize financing cost or choose optimally between a smaller loan, an asset sale, earlier customer collections and a permanent cash reserve. A policy optimization would need admissible actions, state-contingent information, prices, costs, constraints and an objective. Finite scenarios also omit paths outside the chosen set. Coherent combined scenarios matter because deposit runoff, collateral deterioration and customer draws may occur together; adding independently chosen standalone worst losses can describe no jointly possible path.

The funding diagnosis should therefore report both the certificate and its boundary: “39.9 CU before the first cutoff funds this unchanged policy for these three scenarios, assuming the stated receipts and rights.” It should not say “the bank is safe” or reinterpret a three-scenario maximum as a confidence level. Chapter 6 develops process controls and execution failure; Chapter 7 integrates stress mechanisms and their feedback.

Reproducible funding and ALM lab

Download the synthetic inputs, standard-library Python implementation, exact saved output, contract and reproduction guide and four-payload SHA-256 manifest. Put the first four files in one directory and run python3 v11-c05-analysis.py --input v11-c05-inputs.json --output result.json. Without --output, the only standard output is the JSON result. The importable run(data) is quiet and leaves its input unchanged. Rational output strings are exact; for example 399/10 means 39.9 CU.

The lab supplies every journal entry, cutoff balance, collateral inventory, interest amount and reserve certificate for one to eight scenarios on exactly four cutoffs. It rejects malformed or out-of-family inputs explicitly under normal Python and -O. A valid plan with a cash shortfall is reported as infeasible, not rejected as invalid data. Cash-negative diagnostic rows remain hypothetical until a feasible funding plan is supplied. The ALM and currency modules are separate original cases and are not added to Bracken's balance sheet. Change one mechanism at a time, then a coherent combination: remove rollover; delay a loan receipt; reduce deliverable collateral; raise the haircut; remove secured access; or return margin later. Recheck every affected principal and interest payment.

Exercises

  1. Rollover and the final balance. Use worked case 1 and change only the rollover fraction to zero. Reconstruct all four available-cash balances, the minimum timely cash reserve, the ending book equity and the reason final cash is 0.6 higher than in the base case. Explain why deleting the old 40 repayment would be wrong.
  2. Collateral delivery. With principal 30, price 0.7 and 50 eligible units, find the largest haircut that avoids a paydown. At haircut 30%, calculate the paydown when all 50 units are deliverable. If the additional 12.5 originally free units cannot reach the custodian before the call, calculate the paydown when only the initially pledged 37.5 are deliverable. Distinguish both cash payments from a market-value loss.
  3. Journal before aggregation. For the joint stress with no added reserve, show the cutoff-2 entries for the 12 customer draw, 4 extra initial margin, 5.5 secured paydown, −9 variation settlement and 0.3 accrued interest. Calculate book equity at that cutoff, total cash including restricted cash, and the cutoff-2 assets/liabilities identity. State exactly why this is only a full-payment diagnostic.
  4. Prove a minimum and identify its scope. Prove the finite fixed-policy minimum formula, including necessity, sufficiency and the zero case. Apply it to the three supplied scenarios. Give one explicit timing change that invalidates sufficiency without changing a full-day total. Explain why a second cash injection at cutoff 3 cannot replace the required initial reserve.
  5. Value, repricing and units. For the annual ALM book, prove that the reset floating liability is worth 20, including y=0. Derive the EVE and next-year NII yield derivatives at 5%, give the first-order EVE effect of a 100-basis-point rise and the exact EVE effect of a rise to 7%, and explain the opposite NII direction. Does a positive EVE prove that the morning coupon payment can be made when only 0.2 cash is usable?
  6. A different currency transfer. Keep local cash 4 CU and the 12 CU 11:00 payment. The affiliate now owns 7 FU and the quote is 1.2 CU per FU. Calculate the local shortfall without authorization, the balance if an authorized conversion arrives at 10:00, and the 11:00 shortfall if it arrives at 12:00. State what a transfer confirmation must establish beyond its amount.
  7. The bridge loan has a maturity too. Replace the initial cash-equity contribution by a loan of b CU received before cutoff 1 and repaid with interest as (1+g)b at cutoff 4. Hold every other policy and cash flow unchanged. For all three supplied scenarios derive the feasible interval for b when g=2%. Is any b feasible at g=10%? Explain why merely using b=39.9 from the cash-equity certificate is insufficient reasoning.
  8. Critique a funding recommendation. A report states: “The joint scenario ends with positive marked equity; the 20 already-pledged and 10 inaccessible security units can also fund the call; return of all 9 margin is profit; and our 39.9 reserve proves 99% safety at minimum cost.” Identify and repair each error. Propose two concrete pieces of evidence required before approving the plan and one model change that would require a new calculation rather than the old certificate. Use the stated model, without inventing legal entitlements or scenario probabilities.

Complete solutions

Complete solutions

  1. Cutoff 1 is 16+30−40−0.4−10−2=−6.4. Cutoff 2 adds 12−3−4=5, giving −1.4; cutoff 3 adds 18−5−6+3=10, giving 8.6. Cutoff 4 adds 40+5+5−30−0.9=19.1, giving 27.7. The largest deficit is 6.4, so a timely independent cash-equity reserve of that amount is necessary and sufficient under the fixed policy. Without that reserve the full-payment ending equity is 24.6+2−0.9=25.7; with it equity is 32.1. Base final cash is lower by 0.6 because it pays the new term loan's interest. Its initial 40 receipt and final 40 principal repayment cancel over the full window. Refinancing failure cancels neither the old creditor's principal nor the already-accrued 0.4 obligation.

  2. No paydown requires 50(0.7)(1−h)≥30, hence h≤1/7≈14.2857%. At h=0.3, full-pool capacity is 50(0.7)(0.7)=24.5 and the paydown is 5.5. If only 37.5 units can be delivered, capacity is 37.5(0.49)=18.375, so the paydown is 11.625. The late 12.5 units would have supplied 6.125 additional funding capacity. A paydown exchanges cash for extinguished debt; it does not itself reduce equity. Separately, marking one unit from 1 to 0.7 reduces its value by 0.3. A haircut change changes the allowed advance per unit, not the quoted security price. The full-pool and late-delivery policies must not be mixed.

  3. The customer draw gives Δcash=−12 and Δloans=+12. Extra initial margin gives Δcash=−4 and Δsegregated margin=+4. Secured paydown gives Δcash=−5.5 and Δsecured principal=−5.5. Variation gives Δcash=−9 and Δequity=−9. Accrued funding interest gives Δinterest payable=+0.3 and Δequity=−0.3, with no immediate cash. Equity is 24.6−3−9−0.3=12.3. Available cash is −39.9, so total cash is −35.9 including the restricted 4. Loans are 150−12+12=150, securities 80 and initial margin 9: assets are −35.9+150+80+9=203.1. Liabilities are deposits 160−16−8=136, other liabilities 30, secured principal 24.5 and interest payable 0.3, totaling 190.8; 190.8+12.3=203.1. The opening and first-cutoff plan already failed without extra funds. A negative cash asset here records the missing funding in an algebraic full-payment projection, not an authorized overdraft. Adding the specified 39.9 cash-equity reserve raises both cash and equity by 39.9, producing a feasible cutoff-2 state with available cash zero.

  4. With fixed flows, induction gives Hsj(b)=Hsj(0)+b. Any b below the maximum negative prefix leaves that prefix negative, proving necessity. At or above the maximum, every closing cutoff balance is nonnegative; because all eligible receipts precede that bucket's payments, paying sequentially never drops below the closing balance. This proves sufficiency. If no prefix is negative, zero works and is the smallest permitted nonnegative b. For the three scenarios the respective minima are 0, 6.4 and 39.9; their common minimum is 39.9, attained in the joint scenario at cutoff 2. For an explicit counterexample to a coarsened daily ladder, start a day with 0, owe 5 at 09:00 and receive 5 at 16:00. The daily total is zero, yet morning needs 5. A reserve arriving at cutoff 3 cannot repair cutoff 1 or 2; it violates the timely-injection hypothesis. The proof does not authorize transfers backward in time.

  5. The identity y(1+y)−t=(1+y)−(t−1)−(1+y)−t telescopes. Summed coupons plus final principal equal face 20; when y=0 all coupons are zero and discounted principal is 20 directly. For the fixed asset, P′A=−5/(1+y)2−210/(1+y)3. For the fixed liability, P′F=−Σt=154t/(1+y)t+1−400/(1+y)6. At 0.05 these are approximately −185.941043 and −346.358134, so EVE′=160.417091 CU per unit yield. NII′=−20. A 100-basis-point rise is 0.01 and gives a first-order EVE increase of 1.604171. Exact evaluation at 0.07 gives EVE 12.944280, a gain of 2.944280 from 10, while NII changes from 0 to −0.4. Fixed-liability value falls more than asset value, whereas the floating coupon becomes more expensive. These are distinct full-horizon valuation and one-year income effects. With only 0.2 usable before a 5.4 morning coupon payment, the payment gap is 5.2; a positive value residual and a later 5 receipt do not provide the missing morning cash.

  6. The potential proceeds are 7 FU×1.2 CU/FU=8.4 CU. Without an authorized transfer, headroom is 4−12=−8 and the shortfall is 8. Timely authorized settlement gives 4+8.4−12=0.4. If settlement is at noon, the 11:00 shortfall remains 8; only the later full-payment diagnostic becomes 0.4. Confirmation must establish which entity may transfer, availability of the FU, executable conversion and fees, destination currency/account, settlement time and any required prefunding or collateral. A group total or an FX quote alone does not establish these rights. This answer identifies evidence categories, not a conclusion about a jurisdiction's law.

  7. For cutoffs 1–3, the old headrooms rise by b, so their joint constraints require b≥39.9. At cutoff 4, the net effect of receiving b initially and paying (1+g)b is −gb. Final base, rollover-only and joint headrooms are therefore 27.1−gb, 27.7−gb and 3.81−gb. At g=0.02 the strongest upper bound is b≤3.81/0.02=190.5. Thus the exact feasible interval is [39.9,190.5]. At b=39.9 the joint final headroom is 3.81−0.798=3.012. At g=0.10, final feasibility requires b≤38.1, contradicting the early requirement b≥39.9; no loan amount works under this unchanged policy. Cash-equity did not mature within the horizon. The bridge does, and its interest creates a terminal upper bound. This is a conditional feasibility result, not a recommendation to issue equity or a proof that other policies cannot work.

  8. Positive closing marked equity does not meet an earlier payment, and the unbuffered closing state follows an infeasible full-payment path. The 20 already-pledged units are committed elsewhere; the 10 inaccessible units cannot settle the call; only the 50 deliverable eligible units enter new capacity. Returning initial margin swaps a segregated asset for cash and is not profit. The three scenarios have no assigned probabilities, so 99% has no derivation. The 39.9 minimum is for a fixed financing policy and timely independent cash, not a minimum-cost optimization. A repaired conclusion states the exact 39.9 certificate and its rights, cutoffs and scenario boundary.

    Two concrete evidence examples are a lender/custodian confirmation of eligible units, encumbrances and executable delivery before the call, and a dated settlement schedule confirming customer/derivative obligations and usable loan or transfer receipts. A plan using a maturing bridge, a later margin return, a changed facility draw or an asset sale requires redoing the cash flows and, where relevant, principal, interest and book entries. Full credit requires all five conceptual repairs, two identifiable evidence items, and a change whose affected calculation is explained; merely listing “more stress tests” or asserting legal access earns no credit.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain in ninety seconds how a bank with valuable assets can miss a payment, why a collateral paydown and a derivative loss have different equity effects, and what the 39.9 minimum actually proves. Answer standard: identify the entity/currency/deadline and unusable resources; show cash/debt falling together for a principal paydown versus cash/equity falling for the stipulated variation loss; state the finite scenario set, fixed policy, timely independent reserve and unchanged-flow hypotheses. Reject both “positive equity means cash is available” and “all cash outflows are losses.”

Delayed check, after a week. Without the case tables: (1) Initial usable cash is 3 and successive net flows are −7,+9,−8. Find the fixed-policy reserve. (2) A 15 CU secured principal faces 25 deliverable units priced at 0.8 with haircut 40%; find its paydown. (3) An annual floating liability has face 30 and its reset coupon rises by 150 basis points; holding asset and fixed-liability coupons unchanged, find next-year NII's change. Answers: the cumulative headrooms are −4,+5,−3, so the reserve is 4; capacity is 25(0.8)(0.6)=12 and paydown is 3; NII changes by −30(0.015)=−0.45. State the timing, collateral and reset assumptions alongside the numbers.

Sources and next steps

The scoped historical references are the BCBS 2008 liquidity principles and the April 2013 credit-line manuscript. The source record distinguishes reused inspected passages from the additional BCBS cash-flow, contingency, collateral and execution passages read for this chapter. Neither supplies our synthetic numbers or a current national legal rule. The cash-minimum proof, journal, ALM counterexample and exercises are original derivations using earlier taught accounting and finite present-value methods.

Further work can replace the fixed policy by a constrained funding optimization, expand currencies and legal entities, model deposit behavior and contingent actions, or study endogenous haircuts and asset sales. Each extension needs a new specification of rights, information and cash flows. This chapter establishes the dated accounting and finite feasibility result on which those extensions can be built.

Sources and further study

  • Basel Committee on Banking Supervision — Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision (September 2008) — Historical international supervisory method context for timed cash obligations, operational/legal availability and avoiding reuse of encumbered collateral. Not a national-law definition, regulatory ratio calculation or claim that a central bank will lend. Additional c05 use: projected and contingent cash, collateral/transfer execution and contingency planning under explicitly fictional facility terms.
  • Acharya, Almeida, Ippolito and Perez — Credit Lines as Monitored Liquidity Insurance: Theory and Evidence, April 2013 manuscript — One explicit economic mechanism explaining why credit-line access can depend on monitoring, covenant/contract conditions and liquidity states; cash and a headline line amount are not automatically interchangeable.
